findings.description: The inline policy grants full wildcard actions (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) against Resource "*", violating least privilege. Compromise of this user's credentials would allow full control of compute, storage, serverless functions and monitoring across the entire account, including data exfiltration from any S3 bucket and launching instances with attached roles for privilege escalation.

A permanent IAM access key is created for a human-less service user with near-admin permissions. Static long-lived keys have no automatic rotation or expiry and their secret is stored in Terraform state in plaintext when no PGP key is supplied; IAM roles with temporary credentials should be used instead.

No pgp_key is configured, so the generated secret access key is written unencrypted into the Terraform state file, exposing highly privileged credentials to anyone with read access to the state backend.

The output svc_deploy_key_material publishes the access key secret material. Terraform outputs are not marked sensitive here, so the value is printed to console output and CI/CD logs and stored readable in state, leaking credentials for a near-administrative user.

A long-lived IAM user holding wildcard permissions is created with no MFA enforcement or permissions boundary, so a single leaked access key yields unconstrained account access with no second factor or blast-radius limit.
